name: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus — Management
source: American Diabetes Association, Standards of Care in Diabetes — 2024
steps: Start with comprehensive lifestyle therapy (medical nutrition therapy, physical activity, weight management) for every patient.
Metformin remains first-line pharmacotherapy unless contraindicated (eGFR too low, acute illness) or not tolerated.
Individualize glycemic target — generally A1C < 7% for most nonpregnant adults, less stringent for limited life expectancy or high hypoglycemia risk.
Add a GLP-1 receptor agonist or SGLT2 inhibitor with demonstrated cardiovascular/renal benefit for patients with established ASCVD, heart failure, or CKD, independent of A1C.
Screen annually for diabetic kidney disease with urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and eGFR.
Refer for a comprehensive dilated eye exam and a comprehensive foot exam at least annually.
Target blood pressure < 130/80 mmHg and assess statin eligibility based on ASCVD risk.
Reassess A1C at least every 3–6 months, more often when off target or therapy is adjusted.

name: Essential Hypertension — Management
source: 2017 ACC/AHA/AAPA/ABC/ACPM/AGS/APhA/ASH/ASPC/NMA/PCNA Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults
steps: Confirm the diagnosis with properly measured, out-of-office blood pressure readings (home or ambulatory monitoring) before committing to lifelong therapy.
Recommend for every patient: DASH-pattern diet, sodium restriction, weight loss if overweight, regular aerobic activity, and limited alcohol intake.
Target blood pressure < 130/80 mmHg for most adults.
First-line pharmacologic classes: thiazide (or thiazide-like) diuretic, ACE inhibitor, ARB, or calcium channel blocker.
Let compelling indications guide drug choice (e.g., ACE inhibitor or ARB preferred with diabetic albuminuria or CKD).
Start combination therapy (two first-line agents from different classes) when BP is >20/10 mmHg above goal.
Reassess and titrate roughly monthly until the target is reached, then routine follow-up.

name: Community-Acquired Pneumonia — Outpatient Management
source: American Thoracic Society / Infectious Diseases Society of America, Clinical Practice Guidelines for Community-Acquired Pneumonia in Adults — 2019
steps: Confirm the diagnosis with chest imaging when clinically suspected.
Use a validated severity assessment (CURB-65 or Pneumonia Severity Index) to decide outpatient vs. inpatient site of care.
Healthy outpatients with no comorbidities and no recent antibiotic exposure: amoxicillin, or doxycycline, or a macrolide where local pneumococcal resistance is low.
Outpatients with comorbidities (chronic heart/lung/liver/renal disease, diabetes, alcoholism, malignancy, asplenia): combination beta-lactam + macrolide, or respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy.
Routine sputum and blood cultures are not recommended for most outpatients.
Reassess at 48–72 hours; escalate site of care or broaden coverage if not improving.

name: Sepsis / Septic Shock — Hour-1 Bundle
source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock — 2021
steps: Measure a lactate level immediately; remeasure if the initial value is elevated (> 2 mmol/L).
Obtain blood cultures before starting antibiotics, without delaying antibiotic administration.
Administer broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour of sepsis recognition.
Begin rapid administration of 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid for hypotension or lactate ≥ 4 mmol/L.
Apply vasopressors (norepinephrine first-line) during or after fluid resuscitation if the patient remains hypotensive, to maintain MAP ≥ 65 mmHg.
Reassess volume status and tissue perfusion frequently and adjust the plan.

name: Acute Asthma Exacerbation — Management
source: Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA), Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention — 2023 Report
steps: Assess exacerbation severity (mild/moderate vs. severe/life-threatening) at presentation.
Give repeated short-acting beta2-agonist (e.g., albuterol) via pMDI+spacer or nebulizer.
Add ipratropium bromide for moderate-to-severe exacerbations.
Start systemic corticosteroids early (oral prednisone or IV equivalent) for moderate-to-severe exacerbations.
Give supplemental oxygen titrated to an SpO2 of 93–95% in adults.
Reassess response at about 1 hour; consider IV magnesium sulfate for severe exacerbations not responding to initial therapy.
Arrange follow-up within days and step up controller (maintenance) therapy before discharge.

name: ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction — Reperfusion Pathway
source: 2013 ACCF/AHA Guideline for the Management of ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction

triggerConditionLabels.I21.3: ST elevation (STEMI) myocardial infarction of unspecified site

steps: Obtain and interpret a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of first medical contact.
Give chewable non-enteric-coated aspirin (162–325 mg) immediately unless contraindicated.
Activate the cardiac catheterization lab for primary PCI, with a door-to-balloon goal of 90 minutes at a PCI-capable facility.
If timely PCI is not available (goal not achievable within 120 minutes), give fibrinolytic therapy with a door-to-needle goal of 30 minutes, absent contraindications.
Add a P2Y12 inhibitor and parenteral anticoagulation per institutional protocol.
Start a beta-blocker and high-intensity statin as tolerated once the patient is hemodynamically stable.
Give supplemental oxygen only if SpO2 < 90%.

name: Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infection (Cystitis) — Management
source: Infectious Diseases Society of America / European Society for Microbiology and Infectious Diseases, Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Uncomplicated Cystitis and Pyelonephritis — 2011

triggerConditionLabels.N39.0: Urinary tract infection, site not specified

steps: First-line empiric therapy: nitrofurantoin monohydrate/macrocrystals 100 mg twice daily for 5 days.
Alternative first-line: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole DS twice daily for 3 days, if local resistance prevalence is below about 20%.
Alternative first-line: fosfomycin trometamol 3 g as a single dose.
Avoid fluoroquinolones as first-line therapy for uncomplicated cystitis; reserve for when other options are unsuitable.
Routine urine culture is not required for an otherwise healthy, non-pregnant woman with typical uncomplicated symptoms.
Obtain a urine culture for treatment failure, recurrent infection, or if pyelonephritis is suspected, and reassess if symptoms persist beyond 48–72 hours.

name: Migraine — Acute Treatment
source: American Headache Society, Consensus Statement: Integrating New Migraine Treatments Into Clinical Practice — 2021 (building on AAN/AHS acute-treatment guidance)

triggerConditionLabels.G43.909: Migraine, unspecified, not intractable, without status migrainosus

steps: Treat as early as possible in the attack for best response.
For mild-to-moderate attacks, first-line: an NSAID or acetaminophen.
For moderate-to-severe attacks, or when simple analgesics fail, first-line: a migraine-specific triptan.
Consider combining a triptan with an NSAID for attacks that respond poorly to either alone.
Add an antiemetic for associated nausea.
Avoid opioid and butalbital-containing medications as first-line therapy given overuse and dependence risk.
Limit acute medication use to fewer than 10 days/month (triptans, combination analgesics) or 15 days/month (simple analgesics) to avoid medication-overuse headache.
Consider starting preventive therapy for patients with frequent attacks (roughly ≥4 monthly headache days) or significant disability.

name: COPD Exacerbation — Management
source: Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD), Global Strategy for Prevention, Diagnosis and Management of COPD — 2024 Report

triggerConditionLabels.J44.1: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with (acute) exacerbation

steps: Increase the dose and/or frequency of short-acting bronchodilators (SABA, with or without a short-acting antimuscarinic).
Give systemic corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone 40 mg/day for 5 days) to shorten recovery time and improve lung function.
Add antibiotics when the patient has increased sputum purulence together with increased sputum volume and/or increased dyspnea, or requires mechanical ventilation.
Use controlled oxygen therapy targeting SpO2 88–92% in patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure.
Consider noninvasive ventilation for acute or impending respiratory failure.
Assess severity to decide on hospitalization versus outpatient management.
Arrange follow-up and reassess maintenance inhaler therapy after the exacerbation resolves.

name: Atrial Fibrillation — Rate Control, Anticoagulation, and Rhythm Strategy
source: 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation
steps: Assess hemodynamic stability first; unstable patients need urgent cardioversion.
Start rate control (a beta-blocker or non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker) as the initial strategy for most patients.
Estimate stroke risk with the CHA2DS2-VASc score.
Anticoagulate with a direct oral anticoagulant (preferred over warfarin for most patients without mechanical valve or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis) when CHA2DS2-VASc indicates elevated risk.
Consider a rhythm-control strategy (cardioversion, antiarrhythmic drug therapy, or catheter ablation), particularly for symptomatic patients or those with heart failure.
Address modifiable risk factors: obesity, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea, and alcohol use.

name: Acute / Subacute Nonspecific Low Back Pain — Management
source: American College of Physicians, Noninvasive Treatments for Acute, Subacute, and Chronic Low Back Pain — 2017 Clinical Practice Guideline
steps: Reassure the patient that acute low back pain typically improves substantially within weeks regardless of specific treatment.
Recommend staying active and avoiding prolonged bed rest.
Offer first-line nonpharmacologic therapy: superficial heat, massage, acupuncture, or spinal manipulation.
If pharmacologic therapy is needed, NSAIDs are first-line.
Avoid opioids as first-line therapy given the unfavorable risk/benefit balance.
Reserve imaging (MRI/CT) for patients with red-flag findings (progressive neurologic deficit, suspected cauda equina syndrome, infection, malignancy, major trauma) rather than routine imaging.

name: Acute Otitis Media (Pediatric) — Diagnosis and Management
source: American Academy of Pediatrics, Clinical Practice Guideline: The Diagnosis and Management of Acute Otitis Media — 2013
steps: Confirm diagnosis: moderate-to-severe tympanic membrane bulging, or new-onset otorrhea not from otitis externa, or mild bulging with recent-onset ear pain or erythema.

First-line antibiotic: high-dose amoxicillin (80–90 mg/kg/day) unless amoxicillin was used in the past 30 days, there is concurrent purulent conjunctivitis, or the child has a penicillin allergy history.
Use amoxicillin-clavulanate when high-dose amoxicillin is not appropriate per the above criteria.

An observation option (initial pain management without antibiotics, with close follow-up and a plan to start antibiotics if not improving) may be appropriate for select children ≥ 6 months with non-severe, unilateral disease, guided by shared decision-making.
Give appropriate analgesia (acetaminophen or ibuprofen) for ear pain regardless of the antibiotic decision.
Reassess if symptoms worsen or fail to improve within 48–72 hours.

name: Acute Ischemic Stroke — Early Management
source: 2019 AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
steps: Obtain an emergent noncontrast CT (or MRI) of the head immediately to exclude hemorrhage before any thrombolytic decision.
Establish the last-known-well time.
Assess eligibility for IV alteplase within 4.5 hours of symptom onset against inclusion/exclusion criteria; target door-to-needle time of 60 minutes or less.
Assess eligibility for mechanical thrombectomy in patients with large-vessel occlusion, which may extend up to 24 hours from last-known-well in carefully selected patients based on imaging criteria.
Keep blood pressure below 185/110 mmHg before thrombolysis; avoid aggressively lowering blood pressure outside that context unless otherwise indicated.
Start aspirin within 24–48 hours of onset once hemorrhage is excluded (delayed roughly 24 hours if thrombolytic given).
Screen for dysphagia before any oral intake.

name: Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction — Guideline-Directed Medical Therapy
source: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure
steps: Initiate the four pillars of guideline-directed medical therapy: an ACE inhibitor/ARB/ARNI, an evidence-based beta-blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol, or sustained-release metoprolol succinate), a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, and an SGLT2 inhibitor.
Up-titrate each agent to target or maximally tolerated doses, monitoring renal function and potassium.
Use loop diuretics as needed for volume management and symptom relief; they do not replace the four pillars.
Reassess ejection fraction and evaluate for device therapy (ICD and/or CRT) once on optimized GDMT if EF remains ≤ 35%.
Educate on daily weight monitoring and dietary sodium/fluid guidance.
Avoid NSAIDs and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, which can worsen HFrEF.

name: Anaphylaxis — Emergency Management
source: World Allergy Organization, Anaphylaxis Guidance — 2020 update (consistent with NIAID-sponsored 2010 practice parameters)
steps: Give intramuscular epinephrine (0.3–0.5 mg of 1:1000 concentration, anterolateral thigh) immediately as first-line treatment — do not delay for antihistamines or corticosteroids.
Call for emergency assistance and prepare for advanced airway management if needed.
Place the patient supine with legs elevated (unless respiratory distress makes this intolerable) and give high-flow oxygen.
Establish IV access and give a crystalloid fluid bolus for hypotension.
Repeat epinephrine every 5–15 minutes if there is an inadequate response.
Use H1-antihistamines and corticosteroids only as adjunctive therapy, never as a substitute for epinephrine.
Observe for a biphasic reaction for at least 4–6 hours (longer after a severe reaction) before discharge.
Prescribe an epinephrine auto-injector and refer to allergy/immunology on discharge.

name: Diabetes Management in Chronic Kidney Disease
source: KDIGO (Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes) 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline for Diabetes Management in Chronic Kidney Disease, co-aligned with ADA Standards of Care
steps: Preferentially add an SGLT2 inhibitor (for patients with eGFR ≥ 20 mL/min/1.73m²) for kidney and cardiovascular protection, in addition to metformin as tolerated.
Use an ACE inhibitor or ARB at the maximum tolerated dose for patients with hypertension and albuminuria; do not combine an ACE inhibitor and ARB.
Consider adding a nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (e.g., finerenone) if albuminuria persists despite an ACE inhibitor/ARB and SGLT2 inhibitor.
Individualize glycemic targets — generally around 7% A1C, less stringent as eGFR declines and hypoglycemia risk rises.
Start statin therapy for cardiovascular risk reduction.
Monitor eGFR and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio at least annually, more frequently at higher CKD stages.
Provide comprehensive lifestyle guidance: moderated protein intake, sodium restriction, weight management, physical activity, and smoking cessation.
